strengths: The task is useful and clearly motivated: combining a reference person image with a description of changed appearance without requiring annotated training triplets. ITCPR contributes 2,202 queries and a 20,510-image gallery assembled from three existing datasets.

The two-stage framework is practical and understandable. Domain adaptation followed by training a lightweight mapper with frozen encoders offers a straightforward implementation, supported by substantial training details.

The reported improvements are meaningful. In Table 1, the ViT-L/14 text-supervised model achieves 45.55% Rank-1 and 55.26% mAP, compared with 35.38% and 44.08% for Text+Model C. Improvements are also observed with the smaller backbone.

The supplementary experiments provide useful evidence beyond headline comparisons. Table B shows approximately 3.1–3.4 percentage-point Rank-1 improvements from identity-aware CMPM supervision over ITC. Architecture, training-data volume, prompts, and fusion are also investigated.
weaknesses: The main comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. Table 1 explicitly states that Pic2Word and SEARLE retain inversion networks trained with the original CLIP parameters when evaluated with fine-tuned encoders. This creates a representation mismatch and unequal domain adaptation. Retraining these baselines with the same person data and adapted encoders is necessary. Table B partially addresses this concern, but does not establish that the headline gains over published methods arise from the proposed innovations.

The evaluation does not establish an independent model-selection protocol. Section 4 designates ITCPR exclusively for testing, yet Section 5.3 selects network architectures and prompt configurations using its results. No separate CPR development split is described. This leaves the reported performance vulnerable to test-set selection bias, even though training excludes CPR triplets. Together with the baseline comparison issue, this is the main reason for rejection.

Methodological originality is limited. Mapping image features into pseudo-word tokens closely follows Pic2Word and SEARLE, while encoder adaptation and matching losses reuse existing person-retrieval techniques. The task and benchmark are the strongest original contributions; the manuscript should more precisely distinguish its methodological advances from this combination of established components.

Benchmark validation remains incomplete. Appendix B.1 screens potential additional positives using an unspecified visual encoder and top-k retrieval, without reporting k or auditing missed positives. Annotation agreement and results separated by source dataset or modification type are absent. Consequently, annotation reliability and the breadth of the demonstrated capability are difficult to assess.

Some reporting ambiguities impede reproduction. Table 1 presents L_Vis + L_Text as combined supervision, whereas Appendix C.4 describes the corresponding results as fusion of separately trained networks. The exact configuration should be explicit. Results also lack uncertainty estimates, making small prompt and fusion improvements difficult to interpret.

The paper emphasizes public-security applications but does not discuss privacy, surveillance misuse, or the consent and redistribution conditions governing the reused person images. These are relevant documentation gaps for a benchmark intended to identify people across appearance changes.
